Armes1* 1 ASM Scientific Ltd, Cambridge, United Kingdom, 2 Wellcome Trust Sanger Institute, Hinxton, Cambridge, United Kingdom DNA amplification is essential to most nucleic acid testing strategies, but established techniques require sophisticated equipment or complex experimental procedures, and their uptake outside specialised laboratories has been limited. Our novel approach, recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA), couples isothermal recombinase-driven primer targeting of template material with strand-displacement DNA synthesis. It achieves exponential amplification with no need for pretreatment of sample DNA. Reactions are sensitive, specific, and rapid and operate at constant low temperature. We have also developed a probe-based detection system. Key aspects of the combined RPA amplification/detection process are illustrated by a test for the pathogen methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. The technology proves to be sensitive to fewer than ten copies of genomic DNA. Furthermore, products can be detected in a simple sandwich assay, thereby establishing an instrument-free DNA testing system. This unique combination of properties is a significant advance in the development of portable and widely accessible nucleic acid– based tests. Saleh 2,11*, Stefano Ermon3* & Jennifer Dionne2* Raman optical spectroscopy promises label-free bacterial detection, identiﬁcation, and anti- biotic susceptibility testing in a single step. However, achieving clinically relevant speeds and accuracies remains challenging due to weak Raman signal from bacterial cells and numerous bacterial species and phenotypes. Here we generate an extensive dataset of bacterial Raman spectra and apply deep learning approaches to accurately identify 30 common bacterial pathogens. Even on low signal-to-noise spectra, we achieve average isolate-level accuracies exceeding 82% and antibiotic treatment identiﬁcation accuracies of 97.0±0.3%. We also show that this approach distinguishes between methicillin-resistant and -susceptible isolates of Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA and MSSA) with 89±0.1% accuracy. We validate our results on clinical isolates from 50 patients. Using just 10 bacterial spectra from each patient isolate, we achieve treatment identiﬁcation accuracies of 99.7%. identity.title_checked_against_registry: Label-free single-particle imaging approach for ultra-rapid detection of pathogenic bacteria in clinical samples
identity.header_excerpt: Label-free single-particle imaging approach for ultra-rapid detection of pathogenic bacteria in clinical samples Shan Chena,b,1, Yu-Wen Sua,c,1, Junjie Suna,1, Tingting Chend,1, Yuhao Zhenga,1, Lin-Jie Suie,1, Shuangli Yanga,1, Chenbin Liuf, Pengcheng Wanga, Tengfei Lic, Qinghua Chig, Hao Suna, Jinghu Chena, Bo-Qun Xue,h, Zongxiong Huangi, and Yimin Fanga,2 Edited by David Weitz, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA; received April 21, 2022; accepted September 7, 2022 Rapid detection of pathogenic bacteria within a few minutes is the key to control infec- tious disease. However, rapid detection of pathogenic bacteria in clinical samples is quite a challenging task due to the complex matrix, as well as the low abundance of bacteria in real samples. Herein, we employ a label-free single-particle imaging approach to address this challenge. We process holograms using a tailored DL framework that includes preprocessing, detection, and classiﬁcation stages involving three speciﬁc DL models trained on an extensive dataset that included holograms of generic particles present in sterile liquid and ﬁve bacterial species featuring distinct morphologies, Gram stain attributes, and viability. Our approach, validated through experiments with synthetic data and sterile liquid spiked with different bacteria, accurately distinguishes between bacteria and particles, live and dead bacteria, and Gram-positive and negative bacteria of similar morphology, all while minimizing false positives. The study highlights the potential of combining DIH with DL as a transformative tool for rapid bacterial analysis in clinical and industrial settings, with potential extension to other applications including pharmaceutical screening, environmental monitoring, and disease diagnostics. False negative blood culture results due to inadequate volumes of blood can result in misdiagnosis, delay therapy, and put patients at heightened risk of morbidity and mortality from bacteremia. Likewise, the presence of commonly occurring bacteria or fungi on human skin (i.e., commensal organisms) can increase the risk of false positives, compromising care by leading to unnecessary antibiotic therapy and prolonged hospitalization. In December 2022, a Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) Consensus-Based Entity (CBE) endorsed a CDC proposal for a new patient safety measure to address these concerns (see Quality Measures | CMS for more on this topic). CDC developed this quality measure to promote blood culture best practices and improve the laboratory diagnosis of bloodstream infection. The Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments of 1988 (CLIA) state that laboratories must monitor, assess, and when indicated, correct problems identified in their preanalytic systems. Here, an unsupervised learning–assisted and surface acoustic wave–interdigital transducer-driven nano-lens holography biosensing platform is developed for the ultrasensitive and ampliﬁcation-free detection of viable bacteria. The monitoring device integrated with the nano-lens eﬀect can achieve the holographic imaging of polystyrene microsphere probes in an ultra-wide ﬁeld of view (∽28.28 mm2), with a sensitivity limit of as low as 99 nm. A lightweight unsupervised learning hologram processing algorithm considerably reduces training time and computing hardware requirements, without requiring datasets with manual labels. By combining phage–mediated viable bacterial DNA extraction and enhanced CRISPR–Cas12a systems, this strategy successfully achieves the ultrasensitive detection of viable Salmonella in various real samples, demonstrating enhanced accuracy validated with the qPCR benchmark method. This approach has a low cost (∽$500) and is rapid (∽1 h) and highly sensitive (∽38 CFU mL−1), allowing for the ampliﬁcation-free detection of viable bacteria and emerging as a powerful tool for food safety inspection and clinical diagnosis. 1. identity.header_excerpt: | Clinical Microbiology | Research Article Comparative evaluation of BacT/ALERT VIRTUO and BACTEC FX400 blood culture systems for the detection of bloodstream infections Yurong Qin,1,2 Yiwen Liao,1,2 Jingfang Zhou,2 Weijiang Liu,2 Huimin Chen,2 Xiaoli Chen,2 Weisha Wang,2 Ni Zhang,2 Yunhu Zhao,2 Liang Wang,2 Bing Gu,1,2 Suling Liu2 AUTHOR AFFILIATIONS See affiliation list on p. 13. ABSTRACT Bloodstream infections (BSI) pose significant threats to patient health, necessitating timely and accurate diagnostics to reduce mortality and morbidity. This study aimed to evaluate the clinical performance of the BacT/ALERT VIRTUO blood culture system with FANPlus bottles compared to the BACTEC FX400 system in detect­ ing bloodstream pathogens. A total of 1,772 blood specimens were collected from various hospital wards. Specimen selection criteria were based on clinical suspicion of bloodstream infections, ensuring the inclusion of relevant and representative patient samples. These blood samples, collected from the same suspected sepsis patients, were cultured in parallel using both the BacT/ALERT VIRTUO and BACTEC FX400 systems. The diagnostic efficiency of both systems, including detection rates, time to detection (TTD), and sensitivity across different bacterial species, was assessed. In various application scenarios, the VIRTUO system demonstrates a higher positive detection rate, whether in the intensive care unit (ICU) (8.5% vs 6.4%, P = 0.028) or in general wards. Additionally, for different types of bacteria, the TVIRTUO system exhibits superior detection rates for anaerobic bacteria (5.9% vs 3.2%, P < 0.001) and aerobic bacteria (9.1% vs 7.2%, P = 0.043).

Most of the currently known approaches that can address these needs are time- and labor consuming. In this study, we examine the potential of innovative nano-infrared spectroscopy, also known as atomic force microscopy infrared (AFM-IR) spectroscopy, and machine learning in the identification of different bacteria. We demonstrate that a single bacteria cell is sufficient to identify Borreliella burgdorferi, Escherichia coli, Mycobacterium smegmatis, and two strains of Acinetobacter baumannii with 100% accuracy. identity.header_excerpt: RESEARCH Journal of Pharmaceutical Innovation (2027) 22:107 https://doi.org/10.1007/s12247-026-10986-0 Tom Coenye Tom.Coenye@UGent.be 1 Laboratory of Pharmaceutical Microbiology, Ghent University, Ottergemsesteenweg 460, Ghent 9000, Belgium Abstract Purpose Parenteral drugs must meet strict release criteria to ensure patient safety upon administration. Sterility is a critical requirement, and is typically assessed using the compendial U.S. Pharmacopoeia (USP) < 71 > sterility test. However, with the growing demand to reduce batch release times, the test’s 14-day incubation period is becoming a concern, emphasizing the need for more rapid alternatives. Here, we present a first comparison of the performance of the calScreener+ isothermal microcalorimetry (IMC) device (Symcel) to that of the compendial USP < 71 > sterility test. Methods A panel of 16 microorganisms (six USP < 71 > reference strains and ten field isolates) was assembled. All organ­ isms were tested in parallel, in two inoculum sizes (100 and 5 colony-forming units [CFU]) with both methods. Results The IMC-based method detected a higher number of positive samples compared to the compendial method (95.8% vs. 87.5%; p < 0.05). Furthermore, IMC was consistently faster, reducing mean detection times from 43 h to 19 h at 100 CFU and from 46 h to 28 h at 5 CFU (p < 0.001). Conclusion The calScreener + IMC device shows promise as a rapid and sensitive alternative to the compendial sterility test, with the potential to speed up batch releases without compromising patient safety. identity.title_checked_against_registry: Non-Perturbative Bacterial Identification Directly From Solid Agar Plates Using Raman Micro-Spectroscopy and Machine Learning
identity.header_excerpt: Non-perturbative Bacterial Identification Directly from Solid Agar Plates Using Raman Micro-spectroscopy and Machine Learning Jeong Hee Kim1, Jia Dong1, Marissa Morales1, Loza Tadesse1,2,3,* 1Department of Mechanical Engineering, MIT, Cambridge, MA, USA 2Ragon Institute of MGH, MIT and Harvard, Cambridge, MA, USA 3Jameel Clinic for AI & Healthcare, MIT, Cambridge, MA, USA * Corresponding Author: Loza Tadesse, PhD Assistant Professor of Mechanical Engineering, MIT Associate Member, Ragon Institute of MGH, MIT, and Harvard Associate Member, J Clinic for AI and Health Abstract Raman spectroscopy is a promising tool for microbial identification, yet its implementation in microbiology and clinical workflow is still restricted due to the accompanying additional preparation required to focus on microbial signals. Here, we demonstrate Raman-based bacterial identification directly from unopened, inverted agar plates, the same conditions used during incubation. Our approach enabled identification with single gene-level sensitivity using two Escherichia coli variants, differing only in green fluorescent protein (GFP) expression, across diverse media and substrate material conditions, despite the interrogation path traversing 3-4 mm thick background material. We integrated traditional density functional theory (DFT)-based material computation with machine learning analysis, achieving over 97.7% classification accuracy, surpassing the performance of standard measurements from opened plates by 10.8% higher mean accuracy and 0.76% less variance. We further demonstrated Raman mapping-based colony identification via Raman peaks characteristic to GFPmut3

# Cross-review: biosensors → imaging registry

Reviewer: biosensor/applications track. Date: 2026-10-27. Reviewed the 18-record registry structure and targeted two high-risk workflow/validation claims against original full text. This is not a claim to have re-audited all 18 papers or their supplements. No imaging file was mutated.

## Actionable findings

### IMG18 — strengthen culture dependency and validation; qualify manuscript version

**Verified in the legal author preprint:** Methods §2.1 (PDF pp.4–5) explicitly uses Gram-stained smears from **positive blood-culture bottles**, not unprocessed patient blood. Table 1 (pp.5–6) totals **286 patients** and 16,637 images. Methods §2.2 (p.7) already uses patient-identifier-stratified three-fold cross-validation, preventing each patient's images from entering both training and test folds. Replace “clinical n not verified” with a version-qualified 286, and replace “test patient-held-out” as a wholly new idea with external/site-held-out testing. The source contains an “other” class; do not describe its evaluation as having no provision for unrepresented species. Version-of-record alignment and exact reuse license remain pending. [Original author manuscript](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2503.14542)

### IMG11 — time claim is not yet an established end-to-end runtime

The current registry correctly distinguishes reporter-bead imaging from direct bacterial images. Original §4 lists serial capture, processing and reporter steps whose stated durations do not fit the abstract's ~1 h headline: the cleavage step alone is 60 minutes. Preserve “~1 h” explicitly as an **author claim**, flag the timing inconsistency, and do not present a corrected exact end-to-end time without authors' clarification. §2.6 confirms clinical pretreatment and plate screening. §2.3 confirms 99 nm bead imaging but 3 µm assay probes; these are not contradictory metrics. Data Availability states reasonable-request access, not public code/data. First publication is **22 November 2024**, although the issue is 2025. Supporting file: `advs10215-sup-0001-SuppMat.docx` (4.4 MB). Exact CC variant was not visible in retrieved text. [Original Wiley article](https://advanced.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/advs.202406912)

## Registry-level points already handled well

- Distinguishes minimum tested concentration from formal LOD, image/trap counts from patient counts, culture time from classifier runtime, and proposed sensor scaling from measured area.
- IMG03/06/15/16/17 explicitly retain growth/incubation dependence; do not compress their outputs into universal real-time “direct detection.”
- IMG08 labels synthetic-mixture discrimination rather than silently calling it a clinical cohort result.
- IMG10 already calls its timeline theoretical and reports the small positive-case denominator despite larger enrollment.

## Remaining cross-check blockers

IMG09 RSC full page returned 403; IMG10 Nature full page redirected to inaccessible identity-cookie authorization. No access controls were bypassed and those two papers' metrics were not independently revalidated in this cross-pass. Existing license/PDF uncertainty should remain explicit. Author-hosted or arXiv access alone does not establish figure-adaptation permission.

## Taxonomy alignment

Classify the IMG11 acoustic field as an **actuation/contrast-enhancement mechanism**, with molecular recognition and optical bead-count readout; it is not an acoustic binding sensor simply because a SAW component is present. Conversely, S16 nanomotion is a mechanical measurand read optically, and S17 is SAW resonance detected electrically. This prevents mutually exclusive modality bins from obscuring hybrid instruments.

# Independent cross-review of sensor/biosensor registry

Reviewer: molecular branch. Date: 2026-10-27. Target: `../sensors/sensor_biosensor_survey.json`. Scope: high-impact quantitative claims, denominator and date checks, not a full independent reproduction of all 18 records. Source files were not edited; findings sent to sensor agent and parent.

## Required correction / discrepancy flag

**S12 RAPID 1.0, DOI 10.1016/j.matt.2021.05.003.** Abstract reports 85.3% swab sensitivity, but original Table 2 and Results explicitly give TP91/FN18 among109 positives: **83.5%**, with TN30/FP0, accuracy121/139=87.1%. Registry should use table/raw-count result and preserve abstract inconsistency. Saliva13/13 and32/37 (86.5% specificity) agree. Four-minute analytical measurement excludes another four-minute blank and specimen inactivation, already appropriately noted. [Original Table 2/Results](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8106877/).

## Correction scope resolved

**S11 Seo FET, original DOI10.1021/acsnano.0c02823; correction DOI10.1021/acsnano.0c06726.** Correction first online2020-08-28, issue2020-09-22. It corrects more than figure labelling: original clinical specimens were in eNAT, not the stated UTM; replacement experiments used diluted UTM, with repeated LoD/statistical analyses. It also swaps Fig2D/E and corrects spike-protein versus spike-antibody wording. Authors state conclusions unchanged. Retain matrix caveat and cite correction alongside original; do not describe as a verified untreated-clinical-swab sensor. [PubMed correction metadata](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32857489/) / [Author-institution correction text](https://pure.jbnu.ac.kr/en/publications/correction-rapid-detection-of-covid-19-causative-virus-sars-cov-2/).

## Additional qualification

**S16 nanomotion AST.** The clinical interim analysis begins with119 samples, excludes12 screening failures,5 technical errors/elongation and12 incomplete/unverified records, leaving90 complete; first85 analyzed. The stated97.6% is correctly85-denominator accuracy, but not all-started-sample success. Primary Fig4 confusion table gives83/85 correct. Preserve positive-culture start and culture-time exclusion. Main study has disjoint training/test isolates; recordings are not independent patients. [Original paper](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-46213-y) / [Institutionally deposited PDF](https://serval.unil.ch/resource/serval%3ABIB_ABB57C7C3258.P001/REF.pdf).

## Date checks

- S04 Fozouni: first online**2020-12-04**, issue2021-01-21; year2021 may be retained as citation year, but not first-online year. [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33306959/).
- S06 Campostrini: publisher date**2026-01-09**, despite DOI containing025. Targeted cell-count proxies, not species-specific pathogen identification; existing caveats verified. [Publisher](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41545-025-00536-5).
- S13 DEP-impedance: PubMed epublish/article date**2026-08-06**, before cutoff. Matrix dilute PBS; lowest tested concentration not automatically LoD95; existing caveat appropriate. [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42590762/).
- S16 nanomotion first online**2024-03-18** confirmed publisher.
- S07 Nature direct page failed idp500; indexed publisher article-in-press PDF shows accepted2026-01-29 but does not by itself establish exact first-online date. Asked owning agent for existing metadata instead of guessing.
- S08 search lead points to PubMed41626445; exact first-online date needs owning-agent primary verification, not OpenAlex inference.

## Overall assessment

Registry usefully distinguishes instrumental mass/single-particle sensitivity from concentration LoD, surrogate/spiked matrices from patient cohorts, and phenotype from identification. S01–S03, S05–S10 and S13–S18 caveats are generally appropriately conservative. No universal ranking by LoD or accuracy is justified across them. No further paper expansion needed for this cross-review.

## Access log

Primary pages/PubMed were preferred. S07 Nature returned non-retryable idp500; S13 MDPI direct returned429, so PubMed was used. No bypass, authentication escalation or GitHub access. Queries included exact article title/DOI plus `Published`, `85`, `139`, `Correction`; source URLs above preserve the independent evidence trail.

## Owning-agent resolution

Sensor agent reports that the canonical file is now `../sensors/sensors_registry.json` (the earlier reviewed filename is a retained draft). It independently confirmed/applied S11/S12 changes, already preserved S04/S06 first-online dates, and verified S07 publisher first-online2026-02-07 versus Version of Record2026-03-16; S08 first-online2026-01-12. These date updates are author-agent confirmations, not independent re-opening by this reviewer.

# Raman/IR detection research log

Cutoff: 2026-10-27. Targeted narrative frontier scan, **not** a systematic review or PRISMA search. Primary papers, official author code/data, publisher or author-hosted PDFs prioritized. Search performed 2026-10-27 through web search and targeted primary-page inspection.

## Representative exact queries

- Publisher PDFs for Benoit 2024, Tan 2024 and PROGRESS 2026 opened successfully through the web tool (17, 16 and 11 pages, respectively); PLOS RPA PDF opened (7 pages).

- Charalampous UEA repository explicitly lists a legal accepted manuscript (920 kB). Its Download link returned an internal web-tool error; direct PDF URL was not guessed.
- Blauwkamp publisher PDF led to subscription preview. No legal OA full-text PDF/reuse license verified; public abstract and supplements supported only the listed evidence.
- NEJM/Science/ASM lawful PMC copies are not automatically CC licensed. Registry distinguishes public readability and reusable license.
- Python `requests` is absent (`ModuleNotFoundError`); any direct PDF saving uses standard-library urllib. This is a local dependency gap, not a permission denial.
- No permissions escalation or bypass attempted. No operating parameters, primer/guide sequences or pathogen-handling recipes were extracted.
